icePoint.note: The melting point of ice as the table of the source has it, in degrees Celsius. To the tenth of a degree the lab's thermometer is read to, it is 0.0 °C, and the lab takes ice and water stirred together to be at that temperature.

notes.value: The millimetre ruler gave each side of the note one more figure than the centimetre ruler did, and so it gave the area one more. A number worked out from measurements can be no better than they are: a product keeps only as many significant figures as its factor with the fewest.

Ice and water stirred together stay at the melting point of ice, which is 0 °C to more figures than this thermometer shows. So what the thermometer read there is how far it is off at that one temperature. A careful bench writes that down and allows for it. This lab checks the thermometer nowhere else on its scale.

Each scale here shows an edge or a level that is easy to place: a real one can stand anywhere between two marks, and two careful people may differ by one or two in the last figure. That is why a reading within two of its last figure counts in this lab.

Density is mass divided by volume. It does not depend on how much liquid was poured: more of it has more mass and more volume, in step. Different liquids mostly have different densities, which is why one measured density can pick a liquid out of a table.

Every figure in the table is for 20 °C, and each strength is by mass: 95 g of ethanol in every 100 g of the liquid, 20 g of salt in every 100 g of the solution. A bottle whose percentage is by volume holds a different liquid. The handbook table has ethanol of 94% by volume as 91% by mass, which is a little denser than this one.

Two things are taken as simpler than they are. The liquid is taken to be at 20 °C; a warmer liquid would be a little less dense. And none of it is taken to evaporate or to cling to the glass. The volume, read to three figures, is the weakest number here, and it sets the figures of the density.

Pieces that sink push the water up by their own volume, whatever their shape, so the rise of the level is the volume of the metal. Two levels are read, each to a tenth of a millilitre, and their difference keeps that decimal place.

The figures in the table are handbook densities of the pure metals near room temperature. The density of a solid changes little with temperature, so a few degrees either way do not show at three figures.

Some things are taken as simpler than they are. The pieces are drawn alike whichever metal they are, though real copper is red-brown and known at a glance. How much water clings to wet pieces, and how much a drop splashes out, are this lab's own figures. And no air is taken to cling to the pieces under the water.

readingAllowance.rationale: A reading counts when it is within two units of its last, estimated figure of what the scale shows: 0.2 cm on the centimetre ruler, 0.02 cm on the millimetre ruler, 0.2 mL in the cylinder and 0.2 °C on the thermometer. That is a fifth of the smallest division, the allowance the titration lab gives a reading of its burette. The balance shows its figures, and a mass is copied from it exactly.

eyeShiftTenthMl.rationale: How far the bottom of the curve seems to stand from where it is when the eye is above it or below it, in tenths of a millilitre: half of the smallest division. From above it seems higher on the scale and from below lower. Both the direction and the size are the lab's own: the direction is that of a sight line that passes marks on the near wall on its way to a curve further back, and no source was read for either. It is more than twice the reading allowance, so a level read from above or below is never within the allowance of the true level.

tolerancePercent.rationale: A density counts when it is within 3% of the stored figure. Chosen with the reading allowance and the seeded volumes. A learner whose every reading is at the edge of the allowance comes out at most 1.0% from the stored figure for a liquid and 2.8% for a metal, so careful work always counts. No two liquids of the table are nearer than 7.2% and no two metals nearer than 10.2%, so the 3% on either side of one candidate never reaches the 3% on either side of another.

noteLengthRangeE2.rationale: The length of the paper note, in hundredths of a centimetre: 12.00 to 15.49 cm. It is 10 cm or more, so the centimetre ruler gives it three figures and the millimetre ruler four.

noteWidthRangeE2.rationale: The width of the paper note, in hundredths of a centimetre: 4.00 to 5.89 cm. It is under 10 cm, so the centimetre ruler gives it two figures where the length has three, and the area from that ruler has two; the millimetre ruler gives it three, and the area three. No area reaches 100 cm² at any reading the allowance takes, so every area can be written with its right figures and no power of ten.

firstVolumeRangeTenthMl.rationale: The water in the cylinder of part 1, in tenths of a millilitre: 15.0 to 45.0 mL, well inside the scale of a 50 mL cylinder, so that the level read from above or below is still on it.

thermometerOffRangeTenths.rationale: How far from 0.0 °C the thermometer reads in ice water, in tenths of a degree, high or low by the seed: 0.3 to 0.8 °C. More than the reading allowance, so that a careful reading never comes out as no error at all; small enough for a thermometer marked each degree. The lab's own figures: no source was read for how far such a thermometer may be off.

firstMassRangeCg.rationale: The object on the balance of part 1, in hundredths of a gram: 15.00 to 95.00 g, a mass of four figures. About one seed in ten gives a mass that ends in a zero, which is part of the reading.

emptyCylinderRangeCg.rationale: The empty, dry cylinder of part 2, in hundredths of a gram: 60.00 to 95.00 g, about what a 50 mL glass cylinder weighs. The lab's own figures.

liquidRangeTenthMl.rationale: The unknown liquid poured in part 2, in tenths of a millilitre: 20.0 to 45.0 mL. At 20.0 mL or more a reading two tenths out moves the density by 1.0% at most, and the liquid weighs 16 g or more, so its mass by difference has four figures.

waterRangeTenthMl.rationale: The water in the cylinder of part 3 before the pieces go in, in tenths of a millilitre: 20.0 to 27.0 mL, enough to cover the pieces and to leave room under the 50 mL mark for the rise.

piecesRangeTenthMl.rationale: The volume of the pieces of metal, in tenths of a millilitre: 15.0 to 20.0 mL, so 40 to 54 g of aluminium, 107 to 143 g of zinc or 134 to 179 g of copper. At 15.0 mL or more the rise keeps three figures even with both levels read two tenths out, and those two readings move the density by 2.8% at most.

wetWaterRangeCg.rationale: The water that clings to pieces weighed after they have been in the cylinder, in hundredths of a gram: 0.60 to 1.20 g. The lab's own figures, for a film on a small heap of pieces; no source was read. It moves the density of aluminium by as much as 3% and of copper by under 1%, so a run with this error does not count for its cause, whatever its result.

splashRangeTenthMl.rationale: The water lost when the pieces are dropped in and not slid in, in tenths of a millilitre: 0.8 to 1.5 mL. The lab's own figures; no source was read. The rise then reads low by that much and the density comes out 4% to 11% high, outside the tolerance at every seed.
